lines.title: Tokenised funds and money market fund settlement
lines.md:
In this line a bank sells, trades, settles or holds fund units kept as tokens on a shared ledger, such as a tokenised money market fund (MMF) (concept).

## At a glance

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Bank role | Distributor; connecting broker; settlement bank; custodian |
| Client segments | Retail, private banking, corporate, institutional |
| Value chain | Distribute, Trade, Hold, Settle and pay |
| Regulatory gate | Sellers should be firms that the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has licensed or registered, applying normal suitability checks [S:58ea8520974d, para 18]. A bank should tell both the SFC and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) in advance [S:a9aa06fbcc12, para 35 and fn 8] |
| Status as of 25 Sep 2026 | In force [S:58ea8520974d, para 5] |
| Related modules | [C5](#m-C5), [C2](#m-C2), [C7](#m-C7), [E2](#m-E2) |
| Related cases | [Case 5: The board's strategic plan](#case-5-board-strategic-plan) |
## What the bank does

- Sells tokenised funds. The SFC expects sellers of tokenised SFC-authorised products to be licensed or registered firms [S:58ea8520974d, para 18]. They apply the usual client checks and suitability tests [S:58ea8520974d, para 18].
- Passes client orders to a licensed trading platform, as a "Connecting Broker" [S:a64e364fd912, para 13 and fn 4]. It should show a warning when the trade price strays far from the fund's value per unit, its net asset value (NAV) [S:a64e364fd912, para 13]. It should also tell those clients they can subscribe or redeem directly with the fund at NAV instead [S:a64e364fd912, paras 12(b) and 13].
- Settles fund trades with tokenised deposits (bank deposits recorded as tokens). The first focus of EnsembleTX (the HKMA's live tokenisation pilot) is tokenised deposits used in tokenised MMF trades [S:8b67e8dc510f, para 2].
- Accepts virtual assets (VAs) as payment for fund units. The SFC and HKMA do not treat this as a virtual-asset dealing service [S:b79266f3da51, para 7]. The bank should notify the SFC and the HKMA in advance [S:b79266f3da51, para 7(a)].
- Lends against the units. The HKMA says the rule barring client financing for virtual-asset (VA) purchases does not apply to buying tokenised products [S:e64b7b0267b2, fn 4, p.2].

## Revenue levers

- Distribution fees: the fund manager often shares part of its yearly management fee with the selling bank (concept).
- Brokerage: the bank can charge a commission on each secondary trade it passes to a platform (concept).
- Market making: the SFC expects product providers to try to have at least one market maker per product [S:a64e364fd912, para 15(a)]. A market maker earns the gap between its buying and selling prices (concept).
- Settlement balances: cash held as tokenised deposits for fund trades can add to the bank's deposit base (concept).
- Custody: a bank can charge a yearly fee for holding tokens for clients (concept).

## Cost and capital drivers

- Price data: platforms and Connecting Brokers should show an indicative NAV, typically updated at least every 15 seconds in trading hours [S:a64e364fd912, para 20(b)].
- Risk disclosure: they should explain liquidity and price-gap risks and get client confirmation [S:a64e364fd912, para 20(c)].
- Notifications: a bank planning over-the-counter (off-platform) secondary trading should notify and discuss its plan with the SFC before it starts [S:a64e364fd912, para 27]. It should also notify the HKMA [S:a64e364fd912, fn 13].
- Product oversight: the fund manager stays responsible for the token set-up, even if it outsources parts [S:58ea8520974d, para 10]. It should not use public blockchains that anyone can join without extra controls [S:58ea8520974d, para 13].
- Systems: linking token wallets to fund records, payment systems and client reports is a fixed build cost (concept).

## Official signals

- SFC-authorised tokenised retail money market funds (MMFs) held HK$8.66 billion at end-2025, up 14% on the quarter [S:c28638fc5ccc, para 4 and Note 3].
- In March 2026 the public in Hong Kong could buy 13 tokenised products [S:bbd10edd41cf, para 3]. Their tokenised classes held about HK$10.7 billion [S:bbd10edd41cf, para 3]. That was about seven times the level a year earlier [S:bbd10edd41cf, para 3].
- The SFC authorised three retail tokenised MMFs in early 2025 [S:16feb657aaec, Reply (2), para 3]. The Government called them the first in Asia-Pacific [S:16feb657aaec, Reply (2), para 3].
- The SFC stated that the first products under its April 2026 trading framework are expected to be tokenised MMFs [S:bbd10edd41cf, para 6]. It will review how they operate before it considers a wider product range [S:bbd10edd41cf, para 6].
- The 2026 Policy Address says the SFC will promote regulated stablecoins for settling tokenised MMFs [S:ef3648ff1610, para 49(iii)].
- The same Policy Address says the HKMA plans central bank digital currency settlement and round-the-clock operation under EnsembleTX by around end-2026 [S:ef3648ff1610, para 50].

## Industry benchmarks

- The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), 2025 staff bulletin (global, reported): tokenised MMFs on public blockchains held almost US$9 billion by end-October 2025 [I:c1c1a36b00a2, PDF p.6]. That was up from about US$770 million at end-2023 [I:c1c1a36b00a2, PDF p.6].
- The same BIS bulletin notes that some institutional-only funds set a minimum investment of US$5 million [I:c1c1a36b00a2, PDF p.6].
- RWA.xyz, a data provider for real-world assets (RWA), showed about US$14.94 billion of tokenised US Treasury products on 26 September 2026 (global, reported, live data) [I:e258a28e08eb, Dashboard header, 'Distributed Value']. This covers tokenised Treasury bills, notes and bonds as well as MMFs.

## Analysis

> **Analysis — not official**
> **Question:** Is tokenised MMF work a distribution business, or a way to win settlement cash and deposits?
> **How to think about it:**
> - Distribution view: the bank gets a share of the fund's fees, as with ordinary units, plus brokerage on platform trades.
> - Settlement view: each subscription and redemption moves cash; tokenised deposits can keep that cash inside the bank.
> - Cost view: NAV price feeds, price-gap warnings and client confirmations are fixed costs spread over trading volume.
> - Example (illustrative): if the same client moves HK$10 million a month through the fund, the settlement cash can matter more than the fee share.
> **What it depends on:** growth of tokenised fund assets; whether stablecoins or tokenised deposits settle the trades; secondary trading volumes; fee sharing with fund managers.
> **Official signposts:** the SFC's review before widening the product range [S:bbd10edd41cf, para 6]; stablecoin settlement of tokenised MMFs [S:ef3648ff1610, para 49(iii)]; EnsembleTX round-the-clock operation [S:ef3648ff1610, para 50].
> **What this is not:** Not a forecast, not advice, and not the regulator's view.

lines.title: Trade finance and electronic bills of lading
lines.md:
In this line a bank finances trade using digital records, such as shared cargo data, electronic trade documents and tokenised money. (concept)

## At a glance

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Bank role | Trade financier; payment bank; data user; pilot participant |
| Client segments | Corporate, small and medium-sized firms, institutional |
| Value chain | Finance, Settle and pay |
| Regulatory gate | Banks placing customer tokenised deposits should follow the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) tokenised-products circular [S:b2719f3dcb37, fn 1, p.1]. They should discuss plans with the HKMA first [S:b2719f3dcb37, Implementation, p.6] |
| Status as of 25 Sep 2026 | Exploratory [S:eb28508e5032, para 2] |
| Related modules | [E2](#m-E2), [C5](#m-C5), [C4](#m-C4), [B2](#m-B2) |
| Related cases | none |
## What the bank does

- Tests trade use cases in Project Ensemble, the HKMA's tokenisation project. Its sandbox has a trade theme covering supply chain finance and trade payments [S:5f8362ecd97f, p.2].
- Draws on cargo data through Project Cargo x, an HKMA trial with private firms [S:cc2fa9fc0772, para 110(i) and fn 8]. The trial uses the Commercial Data Interchange (CDI), an HKMA data-sharing system [S:cc2fa9fc0772, para 110(i)]. It aims to cut the credit costs and handling time that banks and small firms face [S:cc2fa9fc0772, para 110(i)].
- Explores electronic bills of lading (eBL), the shipping documents that give control of goods. Under a March 2026 agreement with Shanghai bodies, the HKMA is to explore eBL use under Project Ensemble [S:eb28508e5032, para 2].
- Pays in tokenised deposits for corporate clients. For the issuing bank, the HKMA says such deposits should get the operational-deposit liquidity treatment. This applies where they are mainly a means of payment within an operational relationship with wholesale clients [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4].

## Revenue levers

- A trade financier earns interest on the funds it advances and fees for handling documents. (concept)
- Trusted shipment data can let a bank lend with less manual checking, which lowers cost per deal. (concept)
- Payment and foreign exchange fees come with the trade flow the bank finances. (concept)
- Programmable payments release money when agreed conditions are met, such as proof of delivery. (concept)

## Cost and capital drivers

- Controls: for tokenised products, the HKMA expects due diligence, disclosure and risk management [S:b2719f3dcb37, p.3; sections (A)-(C), pp.3-6].
- Compliance: in the 2022 mBridge report, each bank ran its own anti-money laundering and sanctions checks off the cross-border platform [S:947fa49606ab, s.6.5.2, p.30]. Each bank did so before sending or confirming a payment [S:947fa49606ab, s.6.5.2, p.30].
- Technology: links to the CDI, the Port Community System and partner ledgers need building and testing. (concept)
- Legal: a lender needs the law to treat a digital document like the paper one. (concept) The 2026 Policy Address states the Government will introduce a bill on digital business-to-business trade documents in 2026 [S:ef3648ff1610, para 98].

## Official signals

- The Port Community System (a shared logistics data platform) had over 8,000 registered firms in 2026 [S:ef3648ff1610, para 62]. Firms had made more than 20 successful trade-finance applications using its cargo-flow data [S:ef3648ff1610, para 62].
- The HKMA is to study trade-finance uses of tokenised deposits with the Mainland, with pilot deals done by end-2026 [S:ef3648ff1610, para 99].
- The Trade Single Window is to connect with the CDI in mid-2027, so banks can refer to trade data on finance applications [S:ef3648ff1610, para 97].
- The HKMA and Banco Central do Brasil agreed in 2024 to link their pilot platforms to test settlement uses, including trade finance [S:8d9f12b43ada, para 1].
- The 2025 Policy Address said the HKMA and Banco Central do Brasil would test eBL and tokenised deposits for commodity trade [S:cc2fa9fc0772, para 111(iii)].
- In 2024 the HKMA and the Bank of Thailand agreed to explore cross-border tokenisation uses, including trade payments [S:fcea64733871, para 3].

## Industry benchmarks

No reliable industry benchmark was found for Hong Kong.

## Analysis

> **Analysis — not official**
> **Question:** Does digital trade finance mainly cut a bank's cost per deal, or does it open lending to firms the bank could not serve before?
> **How to think about it:**
> - Cost view: data and digital documents replace manual checks. Savings depend on how many deals move off paper.
> - Reach view: trusted cargo data may let the bank judge small firms creditworthy, using evidence it did not have before.
> - Settlement view: tokenised deposits and conditional payments can release money when a shipment reaches an agreed point. In this view, the bank earns on payment flow as well as on credit.
> **What it depends on:** legal recognition of electronic documents; how many shippers and banks join shared data systems; links with Mainland and overseas platforms.
> **Official signposts:** the trade-documents bill [S:ef3648ff1610, para 98]; tokenised-deposit trade pilots [S:ef3648ff1610, para 99]; the Trade Single Window link to the CDI [S:ef3648ff1610, para 97].
> **What this is not:** Not a forecast, not advice, and not the regulator's view.

lines.md:
A bank buys and sells virtual assets for clients through platforms that hold a Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) licence. [S:8a016a912528, para 17]

## At a glance

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Bank role | Broker that deals for clients |
| Client segments | Retail, private banking, institutional |
| Value chain | Trade |
| Regulatory gate | Registration for Type 1 (dealing in securities), plus SFC conditions for virtual asset (VA) dealing [S:8a016a912528, paras 18-19] |
| Status as of 25 Sep 2026 | In force [S:8a016a912528, para 17] |
| Related modules | [C1](#m-C1), [C7](#m-C7), [C6](#m-C6), [D1](#m-D1), [D3](#m-D3), [B2](#m-B2), [E1](#m-E1) |
| Related cases | [Case 4: The night the hot wallet emptied](#case-4-vatp-incident) |
## What the bank does

- A bank registered with the SFC is a registered institution (RI). An RI can introduce clients to a licensed virtual asset trading platform (VATP), or trade for them through one pooled (omnibus) account there. [S:8a016a912528, para 17]
- The RI should offer the service only to clients of its Type 1 business. [S:8a016a912528, para 18] An RI dealing only in Relevant Stablecoins is not limited in this way. [S:a0bd48559762, para (2), p.3] These are stablecoins issued under a licence from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). [S:a0bd48559762, p.1]
- When it only introduces clients (as an introducing agent), the bank should not pass client orders to the platform or hold client money or tokens. [S:8a016a912528, para 21]
- Since May 2026, an RI may deal in a Relevant Stablecoin with its licensed issuer. It may also serve retail clients through a VATP licensed only for professional investors, if those clients trade only tokens the platform admitted for retail. [S:a0bd48559762, para (1), p.3]
- An RI may trade for clients on a shared order book, which links a platform's order book with those of its global affiliates. [S:e64b7b0267b2, Shared Order Book and fn 8, p.6] Retail clients may join only after a clear risk explanation and their express choice. [S:73dac3a5a832, para 17] The HKMA applies this SFC guidance to registered institutions. [S:e64b7b0267b2, Shared Order Book, p.6]

## Revenue levers

- Clients pay a commission, or a spread (the gap between the buying and selling price), on each trade. (concept)
- Dealing income equals client trading volume times the fee rate the bank keeps after the platform's own charge. (concept)
- Client token deposits and withdrawals should go only through segregated accounts at the partner platform or at a bank meeting HKMA custody standards. [S:8a016a912528, para 20(b)] A bank that also offers custody can charge a holding fee on the same client assets. (concept)

## Cost and capital drivers

- Before serving retail clients, the bank should check each client's VA knowledge and risk tolerance. It should also set an exposure limit based on the client's finances, including net worth. [S:8a016a912528, para 20(a)(i)-(ii)]
- Every RI needs at least two executive officers for each regulated activity, each with the Monetary Authority's written consent. [S:8934af8cc884, para 2.2.4]
- Where clients move tokens in or out, the bank should follow Chapter 12 of the SFC's anti-money laundering (AML) guideline. [S:8a016a912528, para 20(b)] SFC withdrawal safeguards then apply on top of HKMA e-banking and technology risk rules. [S:e64b7b0267b2, Client VA withdrawals, p.6]
- Group 2b cryptoassets (the riskiest capital class) take a 1,250% risk weight. [S:9e8d84c87168, Part XII CAE1 explanatory note, column (c), p.215] The minimum total capital ratio is 8%. [S:5d0c13e09312, para 2.1.2] So 1,250% × 8% = 100%: at the minimum, the bank holds capital equal to the whole exposure. A capital charge is set against assets the bank itself holds, so it matters most when a bank trades on its own account. (concept)
- Under the planned regime, licence and annual fees for VA dealing would be set by reference to Type 1 fees. [S:6186c01c6649, para 38] The conclusions also state that the SFC plans to require VA dealers to keep client tokens with SFC-regulated custodians. [S:6186c01c6649, para 26]

## Official signals

- The SFC's list showed 13 licensed platforms at its 29 May 2026 update. [S:b14be2203d39, Licensed platforms table; Last update line]
- Firms already providing VA dealing, including registered institutions, are to get a faster approval process when the new dealing regime starts. [S:6186c01c6649, paras 35-36]
- The Government and the SFC do not plan to treat existing VA dealers as licensed while they apply. [S:6186c01c6649, para 31] The regime takes full effect on its start date. [S:6186c01c6649, para 31] Providers that do not contact the SFC or HKMA for pre-application would have to stop when the regime starts. [S:6186c01c6649, para 34]
- In June 2026 the Government said it and the SFC would bring a bill before the Legislative Council during 2026. It would cover VA dealing, custody, advice and management. [S:c6df52e680de, Reply (3), 'In addition' para] The start date of the dealing regime is not set. [S:6186c01c6649, para 32]
- Under the June 2025 consultation proposals, the SFC would set the standards and the HKMA would be the frontline regulator for registered banks. [S:7395a53cc85a, para 4]
- The 2026 Policy Address says the SFC will enhance VA licensing regimes and issue guidelines that set out a clear path to compliance. [S:ef3648ff1610, para 49(i)]

## Industry benchmarks

- HashKey Holdings Limited (HashKey) runs an SFC-licensed platform. It reported 2025 omnibus client volume of about HK$86.4 billion, against HK$11.7 billion in 2024. [I:786f45f6ea11, PDF p.3-4] This is a reported group figure covering Hong Kong and other markets. [I:786f45f6ea11, PDF p.3-4]
- HashKey's 2025 annual results (group, reported) give HK$522.8 million of revenue from its trading services segment. [I:786f45f6ea11, PDF p.11] The same results give HK$590.8 billion of trading volume for those services. [I:786f45f6ea11, PDF p.11] We worked out the ratio ourselves from those two figures: HK$522.8 million of revenue on HK$590.8 billion of volume is about 0.09%. HashKey does not publish this ratio. It is our own sum, not an estimate by any publisher.
- Coinbase Global's 2025 annual report covers a mainly US business (global scope, reported). [I:6fc50821b9ab, PDF p.93] It gives US$3,322.8 million of net consumer transaction revenue on US$239 billion of consumer volume. [I:6fc50821b9ab, PDF p.93] It gives US$479.7 million of net institutional transaction revenue on US$982 billion of institutional volume. [I:6fc50821b9ab, PDF p.93] Our own sums from those figures give about 1.39% for consumer trades and about 0.049% for institutional trades. Coinbase does not publish these ratios, and they are not Hong Kong benchmarks.

## Analysis

> **Analysis — not official**
> **Question:** How much client trading does an omnibus dealing service need to cover its fixed compliance costs?
> **How to think about it:** Split costs into fixed and variable parts. Fixed costs include executive officers, platform due diligence, AML checks on token movements and record keeping. Income is client volume times the fee rate the bank keeps after the platform's charge. For example, keeping 0.5% on HK$1 billion of yearly volume gives HK$5 million before costs (illustrative).
> **What it depends on:** The mix of retail and professional clients. The partner platform's charges. The share of clients who trade only Relevant Stablecoins. The final costs of the new dealing regime.
> **Official signposts:** The dealing regime's start date. [S:6186c01c6649, para 32] The bill promised for 2026. [S:c6df52e680de, Reply (3), 'In addition' para] New SFC guidelines for VA firms. [S:ef3648ff1610, para 49(i)] The SFC's list of licensed platforms. [S:b14be2203d39, Last update line]
> **What this is not:** Not a forecast, not advice and not the regulators' view.

lines.title: Virtual-asset distribution and brokerage
lines.md:
In this line a bank sells clients products linked to virtual assets (VAs), such as funds that invest in them [S:8a016a912528, para 5]. It may also buy and sell VAs for clients through a licensed trading platform [S:8a016a912528, para 17].

## At a glance

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Bank role | Distributor; broker through a licensed platform; stablecoin offeror |
| Client segments | Retail, private banking, corporate, institutional |
| Value chain | Distribute, Trade |
| Regulatory gate | Registration with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) for dealing in securities, plus SFC conditions for virtual asset (VA) dealing [S:8a016a912528, paras 18-19 and fn 22] |
| Status as of 25 Sep 2026 | In force [S:8a016a912528, paras 17-19] |
| Related modules | [C1](#m-C1), [C2](#m-C2), [C4](#m-C4), [C5](#m-C5), [C7](#m-C7), [D3](#m-D3) |
| Related cases | [Case 1: Virtual-asset custody for private banking](#case-1-va-custody-private-banking) |
## What the bank does

- Sells SFC-authorised VA funds to retail clients as well as to professional investors (PIs) [S:8a016a912528, para 9].
- Offers other complex VA products to PIs only, as the regulators expect, apart from a small set of listed funds and derivatives [S:8a016a912528, para 6.1].
- Deals in VAs through a licensed platform, either by introducing clients or through an omnibus account (one pooled account in the bank's name) [S:8a016a912528, para 17].
- Since May 2026, may serve retail clients through its omnibus account on a platform licensed only for PIs, if they trade only tokens admitted for retail trading [S:a0bd48559762, para (1)].
- May execute client trades through a licensed platform's over-the-counter (off-exchange) service [S:b79266f3da51, para 6].
- May offer stablecoins from issuers licensed by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) to retail clients and PIs. Banks are one of five kinds of permitted offeror [S:7b6c8dc63140, Reply (1), para 1].
- Distributes tokenised SFC-authorised investment products, a role the SFC expects regulated firms such as banks to fill [S:58ea8520974d, para 18]. It can also route client trades in them to a licensed platform as a "Connecting Broker" [S:a64e364fd912, para 13].

## Revenue levers

- A fund distributor may receive part of the manager's management fee, often called a trailer fee. (concept)
- A broker earns commission or a price spread on each trade. Its take rate is that income as a share of trading value. (concept)
- The bank's margin on brokerage is its client fee minus what the platform charges it. (concept)
- The 2023 joint circular expects client orders to be pre-funded, meaning paid for before the trade [S:8a016a912528, fn 25]. Since 27 May 2026, the HKMA lets banks that deal in VAs lend to their securities margin clients for VA trades, under set standards [S:e64b7b0267b2, p.2 and items (1)-(2)]. Cash held for trades can bring deposit and currency conversion income. (concept)

## Cost and capital drivers

- Suitability: regulators treat VA products as very likely complex, so suitability checks apply even without a recommendation [S:8a016a912528, para 5]. Some exchange-traded products are exceptions [S:8a016a912528, para 5].
- Knowledge test: apart from institutional and qualified corporate PIs, clients should be checked for VA knowledge first [S:8a016a912528, para 6.2]. Those without it may trade only after training [S:8a016a912528, para 6.2].
- Retail limits: before VA dealing for retail clients, the bank should set a reasonable exposure limit for each one [S:8a016a912528, para 20(a)].
- Product checks: distributors should do due diligence on each VA product, with extra checks for funds the SFC has not authorised [S:8a016a912528, para 12.3].
- Enforcement: in January 2026 the SFC fined a licensed broker HK$4 million over VA product sales [S:415e4629a80f, para 1]. Between 2018 and 2022, retail clients had traded products meant for PIs only, without a knowledge check [S:415e4629a80f, paras 2-4].
- Stablecoins: for coins from HKMA-licensed issuers, the bank should disclose how each coin keeps its value and how redemption works [S:a0bd48559762, para (5)]. Commission rebates should not be the main reason to recommend one [S:a0bd48559762, para (8)].
- Notice: the bank should tell the SFC and the HKMA before it changes its VA activities, such as serving new client types [S:b79266f3da51, para 10].
- People: the bank needs at least two executive officers for each regulated activity, each approved in writing by the HKMA [S:8934af8cc884, para 2.2.4].

## Official signals

- Hong Kong had 11 VA spot exchange-traded funds (ETFs) at end-2025, worth over HK$5.4 billion [S:c28638fc5ccc, para 4].
- In March 2026 the public in Hong Kong could buy 13 tokenised products [S:bbd10edd41cf, para 3]. Their tokenised classes held about HK$10.7 billion [S:bbd10edd41cf, para 3].
- The SFC listed 13 licensed VA trading platforms at its 29 May 2026 update [S:b14be2203d39, Licensed platforms table; Last update line].
- In June 2026 the Government said regulated stablecoins were expected to launch between mid-2026 and the second half of 2026 [S:c6df52e680de, Reply, opening para]. It based this on the two licensed issuers' business plans [S:c6df52e680de, Reply, opening para]. On 16 September 2026 a Government spokesman said the first regulated stablecoin in Hong Kong had launched in August 2026 [S:8be6d15c6641, para 10]. The official sources reviewed do not name the issuer.
- The 2026 Policy Address says the SFC will improve its rules so tokenised gold can trade on licensed platforms [S:ef3648ff1610, para 49(ii)].
- Banks already dealing in VAs are to get faster approval under the planned dealing regime [S:6186c01c6649, paras 35-36].

## Industry benchmarks

- HashKey Holdings Limited (HashKey), 2025 annual results (Hong Kong and other markets, reported): trading by omnibus clients rose to HK$86.4 billion in 2025 [I:786f45f6ea11, PDF p.4]. That was up from HK$11.7 billion in 2024 [I:786f45f6ea11, PDF p.4].
- Bosera Asset Management (International) reported a fee in its March 2026 Hong Kong fund prospectus [I:d81073907a14, PDF p.96]. Its bitcoin fund currently charges a 0.60% yearly management fee [I:d81073907a14, PDF p.96].
- The same prospectus says the manager may pay distributors a fee out of that management fee [I:d81073907a14, PDF p.24].

## Analysis

> **Analysis — not official**
> **Question:** How do selling VA funds and running a VA brokerage service differ as ways to earn from client demand?
> **How to think about it:**
> - Fund sales earn a share of recurring fees. They reuse existing sales, suitability and custody set-ups.
> - Brokerage earns per trade. It needs a platform link, pre-funding, per-client limits and VA custody.
> - Both need VA knowledge checks for most clients other than institutional investors [S:8a016a912528, para 6.2].
> **What it depends on:** client mix; how often clients trade; platform charges; the number of products the bank offers.
> **Official signposts:** further regulated stablecoin launches after the first in August 2026 [S:8be6d15c6641, para 10]; the tokenised product framework [S:ef3648ff1610, para 49(ii)]; faster approval under the dealing regime [S:6186c01c6649, paras 35-36].
> **What this is not:** Not a forecast, not advice, and not the regulator's view.

lines.title: Roles in virtual-asset ETFs
lines.md:
In this line a bank serves exchange-traded funds (ETFs) that hold virtual assets (VAs), such as bitcoin, as a dealer, custodian or seller [S:c79c4686c5e0, paras 17-20 and 27].

## At a glance

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Bank role | Participating dealer; custodian or sub-custodian; distributor; trading counterparty |
| Client segments | Retail, private banking, institutional |
| Value chain | Distribute, Trade, Hold |
| Regulatory gate | A dealer should hold a Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) licence or registration. A custodian bank should meet Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) custody standards [S:c79c4686c5e0, paras 19-20] |
| Status as of 25 Sep 2026 | In force [S:c79c4686c5e0, paras 17-20] |
| Related modules | [C2](#m-C2), [C1](#m-C1), [C3](#m-C3), [D1](#m-D1), [B1](#m-B1) |
| Related cases | none |
## What the bank does

- Acts as a participating dealer (PD), the firm that creates and redeems units of an exchange-traded fund (ETF). The SFC says PDs of a spot virtual asset (VA) ETF should be SFC-licensed corporations or registered institutions (banks registered with the SFC) [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 19].
- Moves VAs into the fund for in-kind creations (new units issued in return for VAs rather than cash). PDs are expected to transfer spot VAs, held in Hong Kong or overseas, to the fund's custody account [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 17(b)].
- Handles cash creations too: spot VA ETFs may create and redeem units in cash or in kind [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 18].
- Trades spot VAs with the fund. VA funds should buy and sell through SFC-licensed trading platforms or through banks that follow HKMA rules [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 17].
- Holds the fund's VAs as the custodian the trustee appoints. A fund trustee may delegate VA custody to a bank that meets HKMA custody standards [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 20].
- Sells ETF units. For listed VA funds traded on exchange with no solicitation or recommendation, the bank need not run a suitability check [S:8a016a912528, para 9.1]. The bank should still test the client's VA knowledge [S:8a016a912528, para 9.1 and para 6.2].

## Revenue levers

- A PD earns fees from clients who create or redeem through it, and may earn a spread on the VAs it delivers. (concept)
- A custodian earns a yearly fee on the fund's net asset value (NAV), the value of its assets minus its liabilities. (concept)
- A distributor earns brokerage on ETF trades and may share in fund fees. (concept)
- Staking may add a further source of revenue. The SFC may let VA funds stake through licensed platforms or banks, with its prior approval [S:c79c4686c5e0, paras 28, 31].
- Fund reports should disclose staking revenue and the direct and indirect costs of staking [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 28(f)].

## Cost and capital drivers

- Custody controls: custodians should keep most fund VAs in cold wallets (keys held offline) [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 21(b)]. Seeds and private keys (the secrets that control the assets) should be stored securely in Hong Kong [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 21(c)].
- Anti-money laundering (AML): firms handling in-kind VA subscriptions should hold the VAs only at licensed platforms or banks [S:b79266f3da51, para 7(b)]. They should follow Chapter 12 of the SFC AML guideline on those transfers [S:b79266f3da51, para 7(c)].
- Notice: firms should tell the regulators before first letting clients subscribe or redeem with VAs [S:b79266f3da51, para 10(d)].
- Capital: a bank's own spot bitcoin position is a cryptoasset exposure. A bank taking its first position in a new type of cryptoasset must notify the HKMA [S:b7d630146e6c, para 2.1.2 and fn 7]. Group 2b cryptoassets take a 1,250% risk weight [S:9e8d84c87168, Part XII CAE1 explanatory note, column (c), p.215]. The minimum total capital ratio is 8% [S:5d0c13e09312, para 2.1.2]. So 1,250% × 8% = 100%: at the minimum, the bank holds capital equal to the whole exposure.
- Product limits: eligible VAs are only those the Hong Kong public can trade on licensed platforms [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 11]. Funds should not take leveraged VA exposure at fund level [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 15].

## Official signals

- The SFC began taking applications for VA futures ETFs in October 2022 [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 5].
- Three VA futures ETFs listed in early 2023 [S:595215fbed97, Reply (3)]. The first six spot VA ETFs, from three fund companies, followed within months of the December 2023 circular [S:595215fbed97, Reply (3)].
- At end-2025, 11 VA spot ETFs were listed in Hong Kong [S:c28638fc5ccc, para 4]. Their market value was over HK$5.4 billion, up 142% since launch [S:c28638fc5ccc, para 4].
- The 2026 Policy Address states that the SFC will revise its codes in late 2026, in the fourth quarter, to encourage new fund products [S:ef3648ff1610, para 40(ii)].

## Industry benchmarks

- China Asset Management (Hong Kong) published key facts for its ether ETF in April 2026 (Hong Kong, reported). They show ongoing charges of 1.68% a year, based on 2025 costs [I:ee50e4efff6f, PDF p.1]. Its management fee is 0.99% a year [I:ee50e4efff6f, PDF p.11].
- The same document caps the custody and admin fee at 1% of NAV a year, with a monthly minimum of up to US$5,000 [I:ee50e4efff6f, PDF p.11].
- Bosera Asset Management (International) filed a prospectus in March 2026 for its Hong Kong bitcoin ETF (Hong Kong, reported). In that filing, the fund sets a transaction fee of up to US$350 per creation or redemption application [I:d81073907a14, PDF p.120]. The filing says the PD pays that fee to the fund's custodian [I:d81073907a14, PDF p.120].
- Coinbase, a crypto firm, ran a survey of 352 institutional investors in January 2025 (global, mostly US and Europe) [I:233d9b2a0eca, PDF p.3]. Coinbase ran it with EY-Parthenon, part of Ernst & Young (EY) [I:233d9b2a0eca, PDF p.3]. In that 2025 survey, 60% said they prefer crypto exposure through registered vehicles, such as exchange-traded products including ETFs [I:233d9b2a0eca, PDF p.6].

## Analysis

> **Analysis — not official**
> **Question:** Which ETF role gives a bank the steadiest income for the capital and controls it needs?
> **How to think about it:**
> - List each role: PD, custodian, trading counterparty and distributor. Each has a different income source and cost base.
> - Custody income grows with fund size, while PD income grows with creation and redemption activity.
> - In-kind dealing means holding VAs, which brings the Group 2b capital charge [S:9e8d84c87168, Part XII CAE1 explanatory note, column (c), p.215]. Dealing only in cash avoids holding VAs, but the bank then misses in-kind business.
> **What it depends on:** fund flows; fee pressure from fund managers; the capital cost of holding VAs; custody readiness under HKMA standards.
> **Official signposts:** SFC rules on who may act as PD [S:c79c4686c5e0, para 19]; the staking approval route for funds [S:c79c4686c5e0, paras 28, 31]; the product code revision planned for late 2026 [S:ef3648ff1610, para 40(ii)].
> **What this is not:** Not a forecast, not advice, and not the regulator's view.

lines.md:
A bank lends to its margin clients so they can buy virtual assets, and may accept some virtual assets as collateral. [S:e64b7b0267b2, items (1) and (4), pp.2-4]

## At a glance

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Bank role | Lender to its own dealing clients |
| Client segments | Private banking, retail, corporate |
| Value chain | Finance, Trade |
| Regulatory gate | A registered institution (RI) that already offers virtual asset (VA) dealing and securities margin financing [S:e64b7b0267b2, items (1)-(2), p.2] |
| Status as of 25 Sep 2026 | In force [S:e64b7b0267b2, HKMA's guidance for RIs, p.2] |
| Related modules | [C6](#m-C6), [C1](#m-C1), [D1](#m-D1), [C7](#m-C7), [B3](#m-B3) |
| Related cases | [Case 6: Stopping a product](#case-6-stopping-a-product) |
## What the bank does

- Since 27 May 2026, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) allows registered institutions that provide VA dealing to offer VA financing. They are expected to meet standards similar to those of the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC). [S:e64b7b0267b2, HKMA's guidance for RIs, p.2]
- Before this change, intermediaries could not lend clients money to buy virtual assets. [S:73dac3a5a832, para 2]
- The bank lends based on the client's financial capability and the securities or VA collateral the client posts. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (1), p.2]
- Only the bank's existing securities margin clients can borrow. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (2), p.2]
- The bank should first weigh carefully whether relying on VA collateral is prudent. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (4), p.3] If it does, it should accept only bitcoin, ether and Relevant Stablecoins. These are stablecoins issued under an HKMA licence. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (4), pp.3-4]
- Since 2022 the HKMA has said it does not, for now, intend to stop banks lending against virtual assets. This rests on adequate risk controls being in place. [S:642680fa4467, Prudential supervision section, p.3]

## Revenue levers

- Clients pay interest on the loan, usually set as a margin above the bank's own funding cost. (concept)
- Borrowed money lets clients trade more, which can add dealing commission for the same bank. (concept)
- The SFC says financing lets margin clients with strong credit and collateral trade more, which can improve market liquidity. [S:73dac3a5a832, para 3]
- The bank is not expected to raise a client's credit limit just because VA financing is now available. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (3), p.2]

## Cost and capital drivers

- The haircut on bitcoin and ether collateral should be 60% or more. A haircut is a cut to the collateral's value for lending. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (4) and fn 5, p.4] So HK$100 of bitcoin counts as no more than HK$40 of collateral value. [S:e64b7b0267b2, fn 5, p.4]
- Loans backed only by virtual assets must be treated as clean (unsecured) loans. This is because the Banking (Capital) Rules do not recognise VA collateral. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (9), p.5]
- The bank should not repledge or reuse VA collateral, except to enforce it when a client defaults. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (7)(c), p.5] Repledging means a lender reuses collateral to raise its own funding. (concept)
- If the bank counts a client's VA holdings as wealth, its review should cover seven risk factors. These include sudden price gaps, and prices moving closely with share prices in stressed markets. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (3)(a)-(g), p.3]
- The bank should track VA collateral prices in real time. It should also keep a plan for a platform outage. [S:e64b7b0267b2, items (5)(b) and (6), p.4]
- HKMA liquidity rules treat cash loans secured on cryptoassets in line with similar transactions. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 10(b)]

## Official signals

- The SFC called VA financing a first step under Pillar P (Products) of its virtual-asset roadmap (ASPIRe). [S:73dac3a5a832, para 3]
- The roadmap lists margin financing and VA borrowing and lending among ideas the SFC plans to explore or consider. [S:d461c2db6af2, Pillar P, Initiatives 7-8]
- The SFC plans to consult on capital rules for VA activities, including financing, and gives no date. Until then, SFC-licensed brokers give VA collateral a 100% haircut in their capital calculations. [S:73dac3a5a832, para 14]
- The HKMA may revise the haircut with prior notice. It sets no number for Relevant Stablecoins. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (4) and fn 5, p.4]
- The SFC's framework for perpetual contracts (futures with no end date) on trading platforms says they should be offered only to professional investors. [S:49f642bdee28, Eligible investors section] Margin should be cash, or HKMA-regulated stablecoins or tokenised deposits. [S:49f642bdee28, Margin arrangements section]

## Industry benchmarks

- A September 2022 study by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), a global standard setter, covered 19 banks at end-2021. [I:d89ae309f669, pages 104-105, section 2.3] Its "holdings and lending" category, which includes lending to crypto firms, made up about 4% of their reported crypto exposures. [I:d89ae309f669, pages 104-105, section 2.3] This is reported data from a small global sample, with no Hong Kong split.

No reliable industry benchmark was found for Hong Kong.

## Analysis

> **Analysis — not official**
> **Question:** How much lending does a client's bitcoin support, and what does that lending cost the bank in capital?
> **How to think about it:** Look at two tests side by side. The collateral test sets how much the bank can lend after the haircut. The capital test asks how much capital each loan uses. A loan backed only by virtual assets counts as unsecured for capital. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (9), p.5] So the mix of securities and VA collateral in each account shapes the return on capital. For example, HK$10 million of bitcoin would count as at most HK$4 million of collateral, and a loan against it alone counts as unsecured (illustrative).
> **What it depends on:** Demand among existing margin clients. The share of VA collateral against securities. How fast prices move and margin calls are met. Any change to the haircut or to capital rules.
> **Official signposts:** Any HKMA revision of the haircut. [S:e64b7b0267b2, item (4), p.4] The SFC's capital consultation. [S:73dac3a5a832, para 14] The SFC's work on VA borrowing and lending. [S:d461c2db6af2, Pillar P, Initiative 8]
> **What this is not:** Not a forecast, not advice and not the regulators' view.

## Read next

- Module [C6 Financing, shared order books and client withdrawals](#m-C6)

- Module [C1 Selling, dealing and advising on virtual assets](#m-C1)

cases.title: Case 1: Virtual-asset custody for private banking
cases.md:
*Fictional case. All people and firms are invented. Facts about Hong Kong rules are real and cited.*

## The situation

Harbourlight Bank is a fictional Hong Kong bank with a private bank for wealthy clients. Several clients already hold bitcoin and ether, two kinds of virtual asset (VA), with outside firms. They ask Harbourlight to hold these assets for them, next to their other investments. The head of private banking wants to launch a custody service within a year.

You lead digital-asset compliance. The chief executive asks you to bring three decisions to the executive committee: how to run the service, how to price it, and how to cover losses. Harbourlight is also a registered institution (RI), a bank registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) for securities business.

## Cast

- **You**: head of compliance, digital assets.
- **Ines Quaymark**: chief executive (CEO). She wants a clear yes or no by year end.
- **Tobias Lanternwick**: chief financial officer (CFO). He owns the profit and loss account (P&L), the record of income and costs.
- **Priya Harbourfen**: chief risk officer (CRO). She sets how much risk the bank is willing to take (its risk appetite).
- **Declan Tidemere**: head of private banking. His clients are asking for the service.
- **Kestrel Custody Tech**: a fictional vendor selling key-management systems.
- **The supervisor**: the bank's Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) case team. It acts only as the HKMA's published expectations describe.

## Exhibit A: the rules that apply

- A bank that plans to offer digital-asset custody should discuss it with the HKMA first. It should show the HKMA that it meets the expected standards [S:ed61d7c335e7, Implementation, p.2].
- The bank should keep client assets, and the wallet addresses that hold them, apart from its own. This protects them from the bank's creditors [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 6 and fn 6].
- For client virtual assets, the HKMA expects 98% to sit in cold storage, meaning with keys kept offline [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 11(l) and fn 8].
- The bank should generate, store and back up private keys (the secret codes that move assets) in Hong Kong [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 11(b)].
- The bank is expected to be liable for client losses from incidents it causes. It should hold adequate financial resources, which may include insurance [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 11(n)].
- The bank should disclose its fees, and any insurance or compensation cover, clearly to clients [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 20].
- As a general principle, the bank may delegate VA custody only to three kinds of firm [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 14]. They are another bank or a local bank's subsidiary, an SFC-licensed platform, or an HKMA-licensed stablecoin issuer for its own coins with HKMA consent [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 14]. Final responsibility stays with the bank [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 19].
- Under a planned law, banks that safekeep client VA keys would need a custody licence or registration [S:f41a543388bc, para 35(b)]. The Government and the SFC do not plan to treat existing VA custodians as licensed while they apply [S:f41a543388bc, para 48]. The regime takes full effect on its start date [S:f41a543388bc, para 48].

## Act 1: Build, delegate or wait?

Kestrel offers a full key-management system with hardware in Hong Kong. Declan prefers speed and suggests using a licensed trading platform as custodian. Priya asks whether the bank is ready for either.

### Decision 1: How does Harbourlight run custody?

- **A.** Build: run its own key systems and cold storage, using Kestrel's technology.
- **B.** Delegate: appoint an SFC-licensed platform or another bank to hold the assets, with Harbourlight as the client-facing custodian.
- **C.** Wait: offer VA exposure only through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for now, and revisit custody once the new licensing law is clearer.

### Discussion notes

- **Trade-offs.** Option A gives control of the client experience and the key controls, at a high fixed cost. Option B is faster and needs less upfront spending, but makes the bank depend on another firm. Option C avoids new custody risk and leaves client demand unmet.
- **What the rules require.** Delegation of VA custody is limited to three kinds of firm [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 14]. The bank keeps ultimate responsibility for anything it delegates [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 19]. Before choosing a delegate, the bank is expected to check its finances, skills, technology and ability to meet the standards [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 15]. Under the planned licence, faster approval is to go to banks that the HKMA has already assessed for custody and that already provide it [S:f41a543388bc, para 51].
- **What a strong answer covers.** It compares the fixed cost of Option A with the fee paid to a delegate in Option B. It asks who holds the keys in each option, because the planned licence depends on who safekeeps client keys. It sets out the timing risk for Option C if the licence starts before the bank is ready.
- **Traps.** Treating delegation as handing over the risk. Assuming existing custodians are treated as licensed while they apply. The Government and the SFC do not plan to treat them that way [S:f41a543388bc, para 48]. Forgetting that providers who do not contact the regulators before applying may face business disruption [S:f41a543388bc, para 52].

## Act 2: What to charge

Tobias asks for a pricing model before any spending. Declan fears that a visible fee may send clients back to outside firms. Kestrel's pricing is a yearly licence plus a charge per wallet.

### Decision 2: How does Harbourlight price custody?

- **A.** A yearly fee as a percentage of assets held, with a monthly minimum per client.
- **B.** No custody fee. The bank earns from dealing, lending and other services to the same clients.
- **C.** A lower percentage fee, plus separate charges for each withdrawal or transfer out.

### Discussion notes

- **Trade-offs.** Option A matches income to the value held and to the cost of safekeeping. Option B makes custody a feature, not a profit line, and depends on other income from the same clients. Option C keeps the advertised fee low and charges for the actions that cost the bank most.
- **What the rules require.** Fees and costs of custody belong in the client disclosure [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 20]. Before a client buys VA-related products, such as VA funds, the bank should check the client's knowledge of virtual assets [S:8a016a912528, para 6.2]. Institutional and qualified corporate professional investors are exempt from this test [S:8a016a912528, para 6.2]. Each regulated activity needs at least two executive officers (senior staff who supervise the activity), approved in writing by the HKMA [S:8934af8cc884, para 2.2.4].
- **What a strong answer covers.** It sets the fee against a full cost base: keys, monitoring, audit and insurance. It tests Option B by listing the other income that custody makes possible. It checks whether charges in Option C are clear enough for clients to compare.
- **Traps.** Pricing only against fund fees. China Asset Management (Hong Kong) published a key facts statement in April 2026 for its Hong Kong ether fund [I:ee50e4efff6f, PDF p.11]. It reported that the fund pays up to 1% of fund value a year for custody and administration together [I:ee50e4efff6f, PDF p.11]. That fee covers fund services as well, so it is not a private-bank price [I:ee50e4efff6f, PDF p.11]. Another trap is ignoring the round-the-clock security monitoring the HKMA expects [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 23].

## Act 3: Covering losses

Priya asks what happens if a hacker drains a wallet. Tobias asks how much capital the service uses. Kestrel says insurers will quote only after a security review.

### Decision 3: How does Harbourlight cover potential losses?

- **A.** Buy insurance to cover a set share of client assets, higher for online (hot) wallets than for cold storage.
- **B.** Self-insure: set aside the bank's own financial resources to cover losses, with no outside policy.
- **C.** Mix: insurance for hot wallets, and the bank's own resources for cold storage.

### Discussion notes

- **Trade-offs.** Option A moves part of the loss to an insurer, for a yearly premium. Option B avoids premiums but keeps the whole loss with the bank. Option C spends premiums where the risk of theft is higher.
- **What the rules require.** The bank is expected to be liable for losses it causes and to have adequate financial resources, which may include insurance [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 11(n)]. That paragraph sets no fixed share of cover [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 11(n)]. The planned minimum capital for new custodians does not apply to banks, because HKMA capital rules already apply [S:f41a543388bc, paras 41-42]. Rules applying the Basel standard (the global bank capital standard) for banks' cryptoasset exposures have been in force in Hong Kong since 1 January 2026 [S:100b982aadca, p.90]. They amended the banking capital, disclosure and exposure-limits rules [S:100b982aadca, p.90].
- **What a strong answer covers.** It separates client assets from the bank's own positions, because custody standards cover assets held for clients, not the bank's own [S:ed61d7c335e7, fn 1, p.1]. It checks whether the bank ends up holding VAs of its own, for example while settling trades. It explains the cover levels to clients, as the disclosure standard expects [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 20].
- **Traps.** Copying a fund's cover level without checking the source. A Bosera Asset Management (International) prospectus for two Hong Kong funds, from March 2026, reported the cover its sub-custodian must keep [I:d81073907a14, PDF p.118]. The cover is 50% of client virtual assets kept offline (cold) and 100% of those held online or elsewhere [I:d81073907a14, PDF p.118]. That is one firm's contract, not an HKMA standard.

## Exhibit B: illustrative P&L

Harbourlight's custody service in its third year, under each Act 1 option, in HK$ millions. The numbers are invented to show the shape of each P&L. They are not estimates of any market or firm. Net contribution is income minus the costs of running the service.

| Line (HK$ million, year 3) | A: Build | B: Delegate | C: Wait (ETFs only) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Custody fees from clients | 10 | 10 | 0 |
| Other income from the same clients | 5 | 5 | 2 |
| Fee paid to the delegated custodian | 0 | -5 | 0 |
| Technology, keys and monitoring | -6 | -1 | 0 |
| Insurance and loss provisions | -2 | -1 | 0 |
| Compliance and control staff | -3 | -2 | -1 |
| Net contribution | 4 | 6 | 1 |

*(illustrative)*

## What this case teaches

- Custody is mainly about controls. In Exhibit B, most costs come from key safety, monitoring and loss cover.
- Delegation changes costs, not responsibility. The bank still answers for the delegate [S:ce05e67bcdce, para 19].
- A custody fee either covers the full cost of the service, or the bank relies on other income from the same clients.
- Loss cover is a choice about who bears a hack: the insurer, the bank or both.
- The timing of the planned custody licence affects every option [S:f41a543388bc, paras 35(b), 48].

cases.md:
*Fictional case. All people and firms are invented. Facts about Hong Kong rules are real and cited.*

## The situation

A tokenised deposit is an ordinary bank deposit recorded as a token on a shared digital ledger. (concept) The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) started EnsembleTX (the real-value pilot of Project Ensemble) on 13 November 2025. [S:8b67e8dc510f, para 1] Its first uses include managing liquidity and treasury needs in real time. [S:8b67e8dc510f, para 2] The HKMA invites anyone with a real-value use for tokenised deposits to take part. [S:8b67e8dc510f, para 5]

In June 2026 the HKMA held a seminar on tokenisation for corporate treasurers. [S:05369e6084ea, para 1] It said it would follow up with corporate treasury centres (CTCs) that showed interest. [S:05369e6084ea, para 4] Each of these centres is a company unit that manages cash for a whole group. (concept)

Saltmarsh Harbour Bank is a fictional, mid-sized Hong Kong bank. It does not yet offer tokenised deposits. Its largest corporate client, the fictional Pemberwick Tidewater Group, runs its Asian cash from a treasury centre in Hong Kong. The group wants to move cash between its companies at any hour. It asks whether Saltmarsh can do this with tokens. You are head of compliance for digital assets. The chief executive asks you to steer the proposal.

## Cast

- **You**: head of compliance (digital assets).
- **Imogen Quillbrook**: chief executive (CEO). She wants to keep Pemberwick's business.
- **Barnaby Saltglen**: chief financial officer (CFO). He owns the profit and loss account (P&L), the record of income and costs.
- **Petra Tidewhistle**: treasurer. She runs asset-liability management (ALM): matching the bank's funding to its loans and investments.
- **Gideon Harrowmere**: chief risk officer (CRO).
- **Nadia Lanternby**: head of corporate banking. She owns the client relationship.
- **Brightspar Ledger Works**: a fictional vendor selling a ready-made token platform.
- **The supervisor**: the bank's HKMA case team. It acts only as the HKMA's published expectations describe.

## Exhibit A: the rules that apply

- When customers place tokenised deposits, the HKMA says banks should also meet its standards for tokenised products. [S:b2719f3dcb37, p.1 fn 1]
- Those standards expect due diligence on vendors, such as tokenisation platform providers. [S:b2719f3dcb37, section (A), p.3]
- They expect clear disclosure of risks, including doubt about when settlement becomes final. [S:b2719f3dcb37, section (B), pp.4-5]
- Before starting, a bank is expected to have controls in place and discuss the plan with the HKMA. [S:b2719f3dcb37, Implementation, p.6]
- The HKMA's liquidity guidance says when a bank that issues qualifying tokens may count them as deposits or unsecured funding. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4]
- The HKMA's note on distributed ledger technology (DLT) expects the board and senior management to own DLT risks in full. [S:1884530ff235, Annex, item 1, p.2] The note is non-binding. [S:1884530ff235, Introduction, p.1]
- The Supervisory Incubator for DLT lets a bank check its risk controls with a dedicated HKMA team before a full launch. [S:1b1a0de5de5a, para 3]

## Act 1: Is there real client demand?

Nadia says Pemberwick is keen. Barnaby asks whether one client makes a product. Petra notes that Pemberwick already sweeps cash each evening through normal accounts.

### Decision 1: Which first use does the proposal put forward?

- **A.** Round-the-clock cash moves between Pemberwick's own companies, all banking with Saltmarsh.
- **B.** Paying for tokenised money market fund (MMF) trades, where corporate cash sits between uses. An MMF invests in short-term, low-risk debt. (concept)
- **C.** No product yet: join the HKMA's follow-up with CTCs and survey ten corporate clients first.

### Discussion notes

- **Trade-offs.** Option A serves a named client fast, but only inside one bank. Option B matches an initial EnsembleTX focus, but needs fund partners. Option C builds evidence and delays income.
- **What the rules require.** EnsembleTX's first focus covers both tokenised MMF deals and real-time treasury uses. [S:8b67e8dc510f, para 2] Interbank settlement of these deals first runs through the Hong Kong dollar Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system. [S:8b67e8dc510f, para 3] The HKMA plans settlement in central bank digital currency (CBDC) and 24/7 running of EnsembleTX by around end-2026. [S:ef3648ff1610, para 50] The HKMA has noted bank views that tokens usable only in one bank's network add less value for clients. [S:1884530ff235, Annex, item 6, p.4]
- **What a strong answer covers.** It asks what Pemberwick cannot do today, and what that gap costs the client. It separates one client's request from a segment's demand. It checks which uses need other banks to connect.
- **Traps.** Treating a seminar audience as signed clients. Treating the pilot as a finished rulebook. Pricing only for Pemberwick.

## Act 2: What happens to the balance sheet?

Barnaby hopes tokenised balances count as sticky funding. Petra warns that the liquidity treatment depends on the design. The liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) checks that a bank holds enough easy-to-sell assets to cover a short stress. (concept)

### Decision 2: How does the token design treat holders?

- **A.** Closed design: only checked Saltmarsh clients can hold tokens, and the bank knows every holder at all times.
- **B.** Open design: tokens can pass to parties the bank cannot always identify, to reach more users.
- **C.** Payments design: tokens exist mainly to make payments within a client's operating account relationship.

### Discussion notes

- **Trade-offs.** Option A keeps control and limits reach. Option B widens reach and loosens knowledge of who holds the tokens. Option C fits treasury use and ties balances to day-to-day payments.
- **What the rules require.** The guidance covers tokens issued by a bank that is subject to the LCR (a "category 1 institution"). [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4] The tokens are a legally binding claim on the bank, and holders can redeem them in fiat money (ordinary government-issued currency) at face value. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4] Their value is kept stable by the bank's own credit, not by a separate pool of assets. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4] Such a bank may treat the tokens as deposits or unsecured funding, subject to conditions. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4] It must set their maturity by the date holders first gain the right to redeem. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4] If the bank can identify holders at all times, outflow rates must follow the earliest redemption date and the holders' type. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4] Even then, the bank must not count the tokens as stable funding from retail or small business customers. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4] If the bank cannot identify holders at all times, it must treat the tokens as other unsecured wholesale funding. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4] For tokens used mainly for payments within an operational relationship with wholesale clients, the guidance says the operational deposit rules should be followed. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4] A bank holding another bank's qualifying tokens must treat them like unsecured loans to financial institutions. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 5]
- **What a strong answer covers.** It models each design's outflow treatment with Petra before pricing. It checks whether balances are new money or moved from existing accounts. It asks how net interest margin changes: the gap between what the bank earns on funds and what it pays depositors. (concept) It links identity checks to the liquidity result.
- **Traps.** Assuming tokens count as retail deposits. Counting moved balances as new funding. Forgetting the bank's own holdings of other banks' tokens.

## Act 3: Build, buy or partner?

Brightspar offers its platform with a discount for a signature this quarter. Gideon asks who controls changes to the ledger. Imogen asks how fast the bank can go live. The supervisor expects a discussion before any launch, as the HKMA's circular sets out. [S:b2719f3dcb37, Implementation, p.6]

### Decision 3: How does Saltmarsh deliver the service?

- **A.** Build its own platform and connect it to EnsembleTX.
- **B.** License Brightspar's platform and run it under the bank's name.
- **C.** Partner with a larger fictional bank, Corvid Point Bank, that already issues tokenised deposits, and refer clients there for now.

### Discussion notes

- **Trade-offs.** Option A gives most control and costs most time and money. Option B is faster and adds reliance on one vendor. Option C costs least, and the deposits sit with another bank.
- **What the rules require.** The tokenised-products circular expects checks on vendors' track record, systems and controls. [S:b2719f3dcb37, section (A), p.3] A bank issuing tokens itself should take those vendor checks into account. [S:b2719f3dcb37, section (A), p.4] The DLT note expects the bank to update technology risk, continuity and outsourcing policies. [S:1884530ff235, Annex, item 1, p.2] It says shared ownership of a solution could affect a bank's control over changes. [S:1884530ff235, Annex, item 1 fn 1, p.2] It expects the bank to judge whether node operators, the firms that confirm ledger entries, are reliable. [S:1884530ff235, Annex, item 5, p.4] It advises banks to consider widely accepted technical standards so systems can link to others. [S:1884530ff235, Annex, item 6, p.4] The Incubator offers optional live trials, and the HKMA judges any supervisory flexibility case by case. [S:fae36c380174, p.1]
- **What a strong answer covers.** It compares control, speed and cost for each option. It names who fixes the platform in an outage, at any hour. It tests the vendor's deadline against the board and supervisor timetable. It sets an exit plan for each option.
- **Traps.** Letting a discount set the timetable. Treating a vendor's controls as the bank's own. Reading Incubator entry as approval to launch.

## Exhibit B: illustrative P&L

Year-three view of each Act 3 option, in HK$ millions. The numbers are invented to show the shape of each P&L. They are not estimates of any market or firm.

| Line (HK$ million, year 3) | A: Build | B: License vendor | C: Partner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Net interest income on token balances | 20 | 20 | 0 |
| Less: income on balances moved from old accounts | -10 | -10 | 0 |
| Treasury service fees | 10 | 10 | 2 |
| Referral fees from partner | 0 | 0 | 3 |
| Technology build, run and licences | -12 | -8 | -1 |
| Compliance and control staff | -4 | -4 | -1 |
| Net contribution | 4 | 8 | 3 |

*(illustrative)*

## What this case teaches

- EnsembleTX is a pilot with stated plans, not a finished rulebook. [S:8b67e8dc510f, paras 1-3]
- The token's design sets its liquidity treatment. [S:69600121310a, Annex 3, para 4]
- Vendor checks stay with the bank that serves the customer. [S:b2719f3dcb37, section (A), p.3]
- Balances moved from old accounts are not new income. (concept)
- Control, speed and cost pull in different directions in build, buy and partner choices. (concept)

Some of these pages also cover the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) and foreign exchange (FX).

cases.md:
*Fictional case. All people and firms are invented. Facts about Hong Kong rules are real and cited.*

## The situation

Gullstone Quay Bank is a fictional, mid-sized Hong Kong bank. It is a registered institution (RI), meaning a bank registered with the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) for securities business. Driftmoth Digital Money Limited is a fictional stablecoin issuer licensed by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA). A stablecoin is a token meant to keep a steady value against a currency. Driftmoth plans a Hong Kong dollar coin.

Driftmoth asks Gullstone for two things. First, hold a large part of its reserves (the assets that back every coin) as deposits. Second, sell the coin to Gullstone's clients. You are head of compliance (digital assets). The chief executive (CEO) wants one joined-up answer by the next board meeting.

## Cast

- **Marisol Mistlecove, CEO.** Sees a new deposit source and a new product in one deal.
- **Arlo Quayburrow, chief financial officer (CFO).** Owns the funding plan and the profit and loss (P&L) account.
- **Greta Gullwick, chief risk officer (CRO).** Owns liquidity and concentration limits.
- **Dorian Driftholme, head of wealth.** Wants to offer the coin to retail and private banking clients.
- **Driftmoth Digital Money Limited.** The fictional licensed issuer and prospective client.
- **Brightkeel Analytics.** A fictional vendor selling blockchain monitoring tools.
- **The supervisor.** The HKMA case team. It acts only as its published guidance says.
- **You.** Head of compliance (digital assets).

## Exhibit A: the rules that apply

As of 25 Sep 2026.

- Reserve assets should be held in listed forms. [S:240be6833157, para 2.3.1] These include cash, bank deposits with a term of up to three months and certain short-dated public-sector debt. [S:240be6833157, para 2.3.1]
- An issuer should appoint qualified custodians for its reserves. Each custodian should be either a licensed bank or another custodian that the HKMA accepts. [S:240be6833157, para 2.5.4]
- Reserves should sit under trust arrangements that keep them apart from the issuer's own assets. [S:240be6833157, para 2.5.2]
- In June 2026 the Government said HKMA rules have issuers place eligible reserve assets with banks in Hong Kong. [S:c6df52e680de, Reply (1)]
- Holders must be able to redeem at par (face value). [S:240be6833157, para 3.3.1] Valid requests should be processed within one business day unless the HKMA approves otherwise. [S:240be6833157, para 3.3.3]
- An issuer should set internal limits on its credit exposure to each counterparty, including banks holding its reserves. [S:240be6833157, para 6.4.2] Its liquidity planning should weigh deposit terms, early withdrawal options and concentration. [S:240be6833157, para 6.4.3]
- Authorized institutions (banks) are one of five kinds of "permitted offerors". They may offer licensed coins to retail and professional investors. [S:7b6c8dc63140, Reply (1)]
- An issuer using outside distributors should check they are permitted offerors and should assess their governance and controls. [S:240be6833157, para 3.4.2]
- For a bank's customers that are virtual asset service providers (VASPs), the HKMA expects a risk assessment of each one. [S:642680fa4467, AML/CFT section (b), p.4] Depending on the relationship, a bank may need extra checks on the firm's business, its licence status and its anti-money laundering (AML) controls. [S:642680fa4467, AML/CFT section (b), p.4]
- The HKMA asks banks to discuss virtual asset plans with it before launch. [S:642680fa4467, AIs' VA-related proposals section, p.5]

## Act 1: How much of the reserve to take

Driftmoth wants to place most of its reserve with Gullstone as call deposits (money it can withdraw on demand). Arlo likes the balance. Greta notes that one client would then be the bank's largest depositor. Every redemption pulls money out of the same account.

### Decision 1: On what terms does Gullstone take the reserve deposits?

- **A.** Take the whole amount on call, at a low rate, and hold matching liquid assets.
- **B.** Take a capped share, split between call money and term deposits of up to three months.
- **C.** Decline the deposits and offer only the distribution service.

### Discussion notes

- Trade-offs. Option A brings the largest balance but the most run risk. Option B earns less on paper but may be steadier. Option C avoids concentration but may weaken the case for the distribution deal.
- What the rules require. Reserve deposits should have a term of no more than three months [S:240be6833157, para 2.3.1]. Driftmoth itself should set and enforce limits on its credit exposure to each bank [S:240be6833157, para 6.4.2]. Those limits could rule out placing the whole reserve with one bank.
- Redemption pace matters. The HKMA expects Driftmoth to process valid requests within one business day, unless it approves otherwise [S:240be6833157, para 3.3.3]. A strong answer asks whether Gullstone's liquidity plan can match that pace.
- A strong answer covers the trust structure. The reserve belongs under a trust for holders, not in Driftmoth's own account [S:240be6833157, para 2.5.2].
- A strong answer also tests a stress day, such as a large redemption wave alongside a market shock (concept).
- Trap: treating the reserve as sticky retail money. It behaves more like wholesale funding from one client (concept).

## Act 2: Driftmoth as a client

Brightkeel pitches a monitoring tool that traces coin transfers on the blockchain. Dorian says onboarding is a formality because Driftmoth is licensed. You are less sure.

### Decision 2: How does Gullstone onboard Driftmoth?

- **A.** Onboard with standard corporate checks, relying on the HKMA licence.
- **B.** Onboard with the extra checks used for VASPs, plus blockchain monitoring from Brightkeel.
- **C.** Onboard for the reserve account only, and keep payment flows out until controls are tested.

### Discussion notes

- Trade-offs. Option A is fast and cheap. Option B costs more but gives a fuller picture. Option C limits risk but also limits income.
- What the rules require. The HKMA expects a risk-based assessment for VASPs that bank with it [S:642680fa4467, AML/CFT section (b), p.4]. Depending on the relationship, extra checks may cover the firm's business model, licence status and AML controls [S:642680fa4467, AML/CFT section (b), p.4].
- Driftmoth has its own duties. The HKMA expects it to check customers before an occasional transaction of HK$8,000 or more, such as an issue or redemption [S:4d98c6a80b4d, para 4.4]. When it sends a stablecoin transfer of HK$8,000 or more, it must first obtain and record the required details on the sender and recipient [S:4d98c6a80b4d, para 6.5].
- Ongoing monitoring counts too. The HKMA expects banks to watch for frequent transfers to or from virtual asset platforms [S:642680fa4467, AML/CFT section (a), pp.3-4]. Where there are grounds for suspicion, banks should file a suspicious transaction report [S:642680fa4467, AML/CFT section (a), pp.3-4].
- A strong answer asks what a licence proves and what it does not. A licence shows the issuer met the licensing tests. It does not replace the bank's own view of risk (concept).
- A strong answer also tests the vendor. The questions cover data coverage, false alerts and exit terms (concept).
- Trap: letting the value of the deal set the risk appetite.

## Act 3: Selling the coin

Dorian wants to sell the coin to all wealth clients at launch. In April 2026 the HKMA linked launch timing to the issuers' own business plans. [S:193316443831, Follow-up work, para 1] The supervisor has asked banks to discuss virtual asset plans with it before launch. [S:642680fa4467, AIs' VA-related proposals section, p.5] Gullstone books a meeting to hear the supervisor's feedback on its controls.

### Decision 3: How does Gullstone launch distribution?

- **A.** Launch to retail and private banking clients at once, using stablecoin-only accounts.
- **B.** Launch to professional investors first, then widen after a review.
- **C.** Offer the coin only through an omnibus account (one pooled account) at a licensed trading platform.

### Discussion notes

- Trade-offs. Option A reaches the most clients and brings the most conduct risk. Option B is slower but lets controls settle. Option C uses the platform's systems but shares the fee.
- What the rules allow. An RI need not test the virtual asset knowledge of clients in accounts limited to licensed coins [S:a0bd48559762, para (3)(a), p.4]. It should still consider each such client's reason for trading [S:a0bd48559762, para (3)(a), p.4].
- An RI can partner with the coin's issuer or with an SFC-licensed trading platform to offer dealing in a licensed coin [S:a0bd48559762, para (1), p.3]. It should disclose how the coin keeps its value and how redemption works [S:a0bd48559762, para (5), p.5].
- Timing with regulators. Intermediaries are to tell the SFC in advance, and the HKMA where relevant, before starting virtual asset activities [S:8a016a912528, para 31]. The same applies to later changes, including the type of clients served [S:8a016a912528, para 31].
- A strong answer names the conflict. The bank earns on reserve deposits and on sales of the same coin. The sales team may push volume that also swells the deposit (concept).
- A strong answer checks the issuer's side. The HKMA expects Driftmoth to confirm that Gullstone is a permitted offeror and to review its controls [S:240be6833157, para 3.4.2].
- Trap: forgetting that clients who redeem pull money from the reserve that Gullstone holds (concept).

## Exhibit B: illustrative P&L

Figures in HK$ million a year. All numbers are invented to show the shape, not real prices. (illustrative)

| Line | Full deposits, retail launch | Capped deposits, professional launch |
|---|---|---|
| Net interest on reserve deposits | 40 | 25 |
| Distribution fees | 10 | 4 |
| Cost of liquid assets held against deposits | -15 | -8 |
| Compliance, monitoring and vendor | -12 | -9 |
| Technology and operations | -8 | -6 |
| Profit before tax | 15 | 6 |

*(illustrative) Round numbers only. Net interest here is the gap between what the bank earns on the money and what it pays for it.*

## What this case teaches

- A reserve deposit is funding with a direct link to redemptions. Redemptions can pull such money out quickly (concept).
- The issuer's own limits shape the deal. Driftmoth should set limits on its exposure to each bank. [S:240be6833157, para 6.4.2]
- A licence does not end the bank's due diligence. The HKMA expects a risk assessment for VASPs that bank with it. [S:642680fa4467, AML/CFT section (b), p.4]
- Two roles with one client create a conflict of interest (concept).

## Modules to revisit

Module D3 covers anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-financing of terrorism (CFT) rules.
